name: Iris Novak

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to employers, AI companies, unions, parties or government. Your answers stay confidential. Could you walk me through an ordinary shift?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I drive a wheel loader at a large granite mine, filling the haul trucks from the blasted pile. I've got a vocational certificate and enough years on the seat to feel when a bucket is uneven, though I still ask the fitter about anything new. The night premium makes my pay good. My partner Gideon repairs appliances, our children are grown, and the house is paid for. We have about fourteen months of expenses saved and hope I can finish at 65. I don't use AI tools; a notebook and the machine gauges suit me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say paperwork can get quicker as long as the trucks still get loaded safely. A loader bucket does not care how tidy the office form looks.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think my night shift should stay, and Gideon's repair work gives us another income. With the house paid for and fourteen months saved, this picture does not threaten the retirement plan much.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll keep the pre-shift tyre and hydraulic checks and write any fault in my notebook. In the first year I'll ask the fitter to check an AI-drafted fault list before I sign it, if the mine introduces one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel calm about the work and the bills. I could do without another way to put a wrong part number in a report.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What did the loader tell you before the gauge did?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Last spring the loader leaned after a tyre lost pressure, even though the display was slow to show it. I parked it and called the fitter before the next truck came in.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would the retirement payment change?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell Gideon we're still putting money into the retirement account each month. The grown children have their own homes, and there is no reason to change our plan over a faster form.

say: I would accept **quicker paperwork** while keeping loader checks and safe truck loading.
I would tell the office a **tidy form** cannot make an uneven bucket safe.
think: I expect my **night shift** and higher pay to continue.
I think our **paid house** and fourteen months saved leave the retirement plan secure in this picture.
do: **Keep checking** loader tyres and hydraulics before each shift and noting faults by hand.
**Ask the fitter** to verify any AI-drafted fault list before signing it in the first year.
feel: **Calm** about work and bills, with mild annoyance at possible wrong part numbers.
S0.quote: A loader bucket does not care how tidy the office form looks.
fieldNote: Her **night premium** supports higher pay, and the household has a paid house and substantial savings.
She trusts **physical checks** after feeling a tyre lose pressure before the display showed it.

steps.text: Keep checking loader tyres and hydraulics before night shifts
Ask the fitter to verify any AI fault list before signing

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say planning and parts ordering could change before a robot can load trucks. The drivers need a clear way to correct a route that sends a truck to the wrong pile.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think they might push more loads through each night shift, and Gideon and I can afford to say no to an unsafe pace. My own job should hold while robots spread slowly, but I would watch whether overtime stops.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll keep my night loading routine and ask the dispatcher to show me the new route sheet if one appears. During the first year I'll note wrong pile calls and bring them to the monthly operator meeting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel watchful rather than scared. We could cover bills without overtime, but I don't like a hurried truck moving beside my loader.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: When would you stop a truck route?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If a route sheet puts a truck on the narrow west turn, I will stop the loader and call dispatch. A few minutes of waiting is cheaper than a collision.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell younger night drivers?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the younger night drivers to keep records of bad route calls. I wouldn't tell them to leave; there are several mines nearby, but each still pays its own way.

say: I would expect **planning and ordering** to change before robots handle the loader.
I would insist drivers can **correct routes** that send trucks to the wrong pile.
think: I expect my **loader post** to hold, though overtime may become less reliable.
I think our savings let us reject an **unsafe pace** without risking next month’s bills.
do: **Keep loading** night trucks and ask dispatch about any new route sheet.
**Record wrong pile calls** and raise them at the monthly operator meeting during the first year.
feel: **Watchful** of faster traffic near the loader, with household bills protected.
S1.quote: A few minutes of waiting is cheaper than a collision.
fieldNote: She sees **thinking-task changes** in routes and parts before capable robots take over loading.
Her **financial cushion** lets her challenge unsafe pace; possible overtime loss would not threaten basic bills.

steps.text: Keep loading night trucks while checking new route sheets
Raise recorded wrong pile calls at the operator meeting

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the crew thinking AI by 2028 may change dispatch and reports, while loader robots arrive around 2031 in this picture. I need wages until 65, so I want the mine to give drivers a clear date for any roster change.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be 63 when capable robots arrive, two years short of my planned finish. Fourteen months of savings could bridge part of a gap, but losing the night premium could reduce the retirement money we hoped to put aside.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll ask the retirement office this month to calculate my income at 63 and at 65, including the night premium. In the first year after thinking AI arrives, I'll keep loading if shifts exist and seek another loader post at a nearby mine if our roster is cut.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious about the last two earning years, even with savings. I can drive a loader elsewhere, but I cannot replace a missed pension contribution by wishing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which plan would you pause at home?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell Gideon we should hold off paying for the long rail trip until we know the roster. We can afford a short break, but not a bet on my last two years of night pay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you take a robot inspection post?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask the fitter whether robots still need an operator to check buckets and tyres. I would consider that work only if the hours and pay are close enough to keep our retirement payments.

say: I would distinguish **2028 dispatch AI** from capable loader robots around 2031.
I would request a **roster date** because I need two more years of wages to reach 65.
think: I think at **63**, robots could remove night shifts before my planned retirement.
I think fourteen months saved helps, but lost **night premium** could shrink final pension contributions.
do: **Request retirement figures** for ages 63 and 65, including night pay.
**Seek** a nearby loader post in the first year after thinking AI arrives if the mine cuts my roster.
**Delay** our long rail trip until the loader roster is clear.
feel: **Anxious** about losing two earning years, though savings and nearby mines give options.
S2.quote: I cannot replace a missed pension contribution by wishing.
fieldNote: She calculates **2031 robot arrival** at age 63, two years before her intended retirement.
Her **nearby job search** depends on an actual roster cut; night premium and pension payments determine the shortfall.

steps.text: Request retirement figures at 63 and 65 including night pay
Seek a nearby loader post if the mine cuts night shifts
Delay the long rail trip until the loader roster is clear

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say thinking AI by 2031 may change the route sheets, but capable loader robots come around 2034. If the loader work lasts to 65, the machines arrive after I plan to finish.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be 63 when thinking AI arrives and 66 when robots do. We have saved enough to handle a short gap, though I will not resign until I have the pension figure in writing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll keep loading and put my night premium into retirement savings until 65, if the shifts continue. In the first year after thinking AI arrives, I'll check the pension statement and set a retirement date only if the amount covers our usual bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel mostly calm because this picture puts the robot date after my planned retirement. The night shift is still work I must keep doing safely until the numbers are settled.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if night shifts end a year early?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If the mine cuts my nights at 64, I would look at another loader vacancy before drawing the pension early. A nearby mine might have a shift, but I would need an offer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: When would you tell your children a date?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell our grown children the date once Gideon and I have made it real. I won't invite them to plan a family trip around a pension estimate.

say: I would note **2034 robots** arrive after my hoped-for retirement at 65.
I would wait for a **written pension figure** before announcing a retirement date.
think: I think at **63** when thinking AI arrives, I still expect two working years.
I think our **savings** cover a short gap, but I will not resign on an estimate.
do: **Keep loading** and put night premium into retirement savings until 65 if shifts continue.
**Set a retirement date** after thinking AI arrives only if the written pension covers normal bills.
feel: **Mostly calm** because robots arrive after her planned finish, while safe work and pension checks still matter.
S3.quote: I will not resign until I have the pension figure in writing.
fieldNote: Her **2034 age** is 66, after her hoped-for retirement at 65.
She keeps the **retirement date conditional** on continued shifts and a written pension amount covering routine bills.

steps.text: Keep loading night shifts and saving the premium until 65 if shifts continue
Set a retirement date only if written pension income covers normal bills

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say thinking AI by 2036 and loader robots around 2039 are dates for younger drivers to plan around. I should be retired before either one if the mine keeps its present shifts and my pension covers our bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be 68 when thinking AI arrives and 71 when robots come. Our fourteen months saved and the paid house make retirement at 65 plausible, though I still want to see the pension statement before putting in notice.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll keep loading carefully and paying the retirement account while shifts last. In the first year after thinking AI arrives, if I have retired as planned, I'll check our annual pension budget with Gideon rather than go looking for another mine post.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel calm about my own job and home in this longer picture. I still hope the younger drivers get enough warning before a roster changes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the pension is below your estimate?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If my pension comes in lower than expected at 65, I would ask about another night shift nearby before retiring. I would rather work another loader year than drain our household savings in one year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell a new loader operator?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell a new loader operator to learn the weight of the bucket before trusting an automatic indicator. A machine can show a number; the operator has to keep the truck upright.

say: I would expect **2036 AI** and 2039 loader robots after my hoped-for retirement.
I would tell younger drivers to seek **clear roster notice** while learning the physical loader work.
think: I think at **68** and then 71, I expect to be retired if pension figures support our plan.
I think the **paid house** and fourteen months saved make a shortfall manageable without ignoring the figures.
do: **Keep loading** and paying into retirement while shifts last.
**Review the pension budget** with Gideon after thinking AI arrives if retired as planned.
feel: **Calm** about her own household, with concern for younger drivers facing later robot changes.
S4.quote: I would rather work another loader year than drain our household savings in one year.
fieldNote: Her **2036 and 2039 ages** are 68 and 71, so her planned retirement comes first.
She will **work longer** if the pension is too low, using nearby loader jobs before consuming savings rapidly.

steps.text: Keep loading night shifts and paying into retirement while work lasts
Review annual pension income against household bills if retired after 2036

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because loader robots might arrive around 2031, when I would be 63 and still hoping for two years of night pay. A written roster date and pension figures at 63 and 65 would let Gideon and me plan the gap.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask what the night premium has meant for us. The loader night premium paid for our house without leaving debts for our children. I want the last years of that pay to build retirement savings.

headlineQuote: The loader night premium paid for our house without leaving debts for our children.
portrait: **Iris Novak**, 58, drives a wheel loader at a large granite mine and has a vocational certificate.
Her **night premium** brings higher pay; she and her partner have a paid house and fourteen months of savings.
She does **not use AI** and prefers familiar checks, though she will inspect new route sheets with dispatch.
Her target is **retirement at 65**, making a 2031 robot date a threat to two final earning years.
With **2034 or 2039 robots**, she expects retirement first, provided written pension income covers ordinary bills.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** worries her most because capable loader robots could arrive at 63, two years before intended retirement.
whatWouldHelp: A **written roster date** and pension figures at ages 63 and 65 would help her plan any gap.
